summary: Lists security threats related to IPv6 multihoming. Multihoming may create opportunities to redirect packets to unintended addresses. The document looks at threats common to all solutions. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IPv6 multihoming lets a site use several Internet connections or switch between them. This RFC explains how attackers might exploit those changes to redirect, disrupt or observe traffic.

questions: what security threats does ipv6 multihoming create
subtitle: The security risks created when IPv6 sites use more than one network path

tldr.problem: A multihomed site can change the network path used by an ongoing connection. An attacker may exploit that change to send traffic to an unintended location.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs threats that apply across multihoming designs, including redirection, black holes, denial of service against third parties, packet injection and privacy loss.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC gives designers a threat list, not a solution or a complete analysis of any particular design.

today: RFC 4218 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the document itself says a specific multihoming design needs its own threat analysis.

sections.title: Why Multihoming Raises Security Questions
sections.content:
IPv6 multihoming aims to let a site use several connections to the Internet, at the same time or as alternatives after a failure, without adding a separate site entry to global routing. A multihoming design may separate a host's identity from its current network location.

The main risk is redirection: an attacker may cause packets for a connection to go somewhere other than the peer expected by the transport or application. This can expose or alter data, or stop it from arriving. The RFC catalogs general threats rather than analyzing one proposed design.
sections.plainLanguage: Multihoming lets a site use several Internet paths or switch paths after a failure. A design must prevent attackers from using those changes to send a connection's traffic to the wrong place.

sections.title: Attacker Capabilities and Identity
sections.content:
The analysis treats an on-path attacker as able to observe, inject and block packets. An off-path attacker cannot observe or block the connection, but may send packets with arbitrary source addresses; ingress filtering can limit that ability. These are simplifying assumptions for comparing threats.

A design needs to distinguish a peer's identity from the network location used to reach it. The RFC describes this as authenticating a peer and checking its authority to use a locator, or as proving ownership of an identifier to control its locators. Security protections already used by an application should not become weaker when a path changes.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker on the route can see, change or block packets; an attacker elsewhere can try to send forged packets. The design must verify that a new network location belongs to the peer already in the conversation.

sections.title: Redirection, Black Holes and Denial of Service
sections.content:
An attacker may try to redirect an existing flow to the attacker's own location, or install false location information before communication begins. Replaying old information after a site renumbers can also direct packets to a location that no longer belongs to the peer. Redirecting packets to an unreachable location creates a black-hole attack.

A redirection can also make one host send traffic to an unrelated third party, hiding the attacker and potentially amplifying a denial-of-service attack. The RFC discusses checking that a peer controls a proposed location, using replay protection and periodically verifying that a peer remains reachable. These are design considerations, not a defined protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: False location information can send packets to an attacker, make them disappear or turn a host into an unwitting source of traffic against someone else. A design needs to verify new locations and protect its updates against replay.

sections.title: Unknown Locations and Privacy
sections.content:
A multihoming design must decide whether to accept packets from a source location it has not verified. Rejecting every unfamiliar location may be too strict, since ingress filtering is not universal; accepting them may make packet injection easier. The RFC notes that IPsec can reject spoofed packets above the multihoming layer, but redirection may still cause denial of service.

Sharing several locators with a peer can make it easier to correlate a host's locations over time. Signaling may also expose those locations to observers on the path. The RFC suggests that designers consider privacy-preserving identifiers and the consequences of making locator information visible.
sections.plainLanguage: Accepting packets from a new location can help a connection continue, but it can also make forged packets easier to use. Sharing several locations may let observers connect a host's activity across networks.

sections.title: Scope and Remaining Analysis
sections.content:
The threats depend partly on where a solution operates. A network-layer mechanism may redirect traffic for an address, while a transport-layer mechanism may affect only one connection. The RFC says that the security impact of state lifetime, direction and host movement remains difficult to assess.

This analysis does not cover multicast-specific threats, connectionless transports in depth, or attacks against a proposed identifier-to-locator binding mechanism. Each actual design needs its own analysis. Physical access to network equipment and endpoints is also outside the document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC is a starting point, not a complete security review. Each multihoming design needs to examine its own mechanisms, including how long location information lasts and what happens when a host moves.
